people.label: Gordon Gray
people.sub: First Director of the Psychological Strategy Board, appointed 1951; Secretary of the Army 1949-50; Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs 1958-61
people.narrative: Gordon Gray held, in sequence, four offices that between them cover the whole of this board's early period: Secretary of the Army, first Director of the Psychological Strategy Board, Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs, and Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs. The Psychological Strategy Board is the one that matters here. President Truman established it by a secret directive of 4 April 1951 to coordinate the psychological operations of the whole government, sitting a Board of the Under Secretary of State, the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence over a Director designated by the President, and Gray was that Director. The directive gives the Director a claim on the participating departments for assistance and access to information, and in the same breath forbids the Board and the Director to conduct any psychological operations themselves. Gray reaches this corpus only as a name inside the MJ-12 attribution, and none of the documents opened here bears on that; the reason to carry him is the office.

He reaches this board as the addressee of the memorandum the whole MJ-12 corpus is built on and as the subject of a recurring claim that his death was concealed. people.label: Rear Adm. Sidney W. Souers
people.sub: First Director of Central Intelligence, Central Intelligence Group, 1946; first Executive Secretary, National Security Council, 1947-1950
people.narrative: Souers held, in sequence, the two offices through which the postwar national security paper actually moved. He was the first Director of Central Intelligence, designated under the Presidential directive of 22 January 1946 that created the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group, and he served until 10 June 1946. From August 1947 he was the first Executive Secretary of the National Security Council, the civilian staff head the National Security Act of 1947 created by statute, and he held that post until January 1950. At the Council's first meeting on 26 September 1947 the Council routed attendance requests and meeting scheduling through him, gave him full powers over its funds, resolved that its affairs would be conducted with the utmost secrecy, and admitted the Director of Central Intelligence as an observer and adviser. The board argues at length about what the National Security Council was and was not shown and has no node for the man who built its secretariat. He is named in the MJ-12 Eisenhower Briefing Document, and that is not why he is here.

people.label: James Jesus Angleton
people.sub: Chief, CIA Counterintelligence Staff, 1954-1974; ran the covert mail programme 1955-1973
people.narrative: Angleton was Chief of the CIA's Counterintelligence Staff from 1954 to 1974 and, on the Church Committee's finding, in charge of the Agency's covert mail programme from 1955 until its termination in 1973. In November 1955 he proposed moving the New York mail intercept from photographing envelopes to opening them, indexing and analysing the product, and shifting primary responsibility for the project from the Office of Security to his own staff. The Committee found that the project was never processed through the Agency's approval system, had no separate funds, and in twenty years was reviewed by disinterested components twice, both reviews' recommendations going unimplemented. Angleton's own explanation was that normal processing would have opened the activity to too many people, and that the arrangement short-circuited the project approval process. He is carried here as a documented precedent for records and activities held outside an agency's own approval and review machinery, and for nothing else: nothing in the Church Committee record connects him to any UFO-related holding.

entities.label: Institute of Field Physics (UNC Chapel Hill)
entities.sub: Privately endowed gravitation-research institute inside the UNC physics department, incorporated 7 September 1955
entities.desc: The Institute of Field Physics received its certificate of incorporation on 7 September 1955 and was placed inside the physics department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, directed by Bryce and Cecile DeWitt and funded principally by the Winston-Salem industrialist Agnew Bahnson. Its inaugural event was the Conference on the Role of Gravitation in Physics at Chapel Hill in January 1957, now known as GR1. It sits on the same money as the board's existing Martin thread: George Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company bought a Founder's Membership for $5,000 while the company was separately standing up RIAS, whose first researcher was Louis Witten. The thing a node must carry is what the Institute wrote about itself. On John Wheeler's insistence a 'Protection Clause' was attached to every IOFP publicity statement declaring that the work 'has no connection with so-called "anti-gravity research" of whatever kind and for whatever purposes', and the department's own history says the instruction to avoid anti-gravity connotations runs through the founding correspondence like a mantra.

claims.text: The Institute was incorporated and sited deliberately inside a university: 'The IOFP received its certificate of incorporation on September 7, 1955.' 'The plan of the IOFP was to house an institute within an academic institution, so as to avoid the conflict that physicists felt working in an industrial setting. The chosen location was the physics department at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.'

entities.label: Deep Submergence Systems Project (DSSP)
entities.sub: US Navy project for deep-ocean rescue, search, salvage and recovery, established 1964 in the Special Projects Office
entities.desc: DSSP is the documented Navy organisation behind the deep-ocean recovery capability the Area 52 corpus talks about, and the board's undersea thread currently has no office at all. The Deep-Submergence Systems Review Group was established in April 1963, after the loss of USS Thresher, to review Navy plans for the location, identification, rescue from and recovery of deep-submerged large objects from the ocean floor. It reported in February 1964, and the Secretary of the Navy assigned implementation of the resulting programme, renamed the Deep-Submergence Systems Project, to the Navy's Special Projects Office; by 1967 it was a separate project within the Naval Material Command. Its two primary objectives were rescue of personnel from distressed submarines and locating and recovering small objects from the ocean depths, pursued through a rescue vehicle rated for 6,000 feet and a separate search vehicle intended to search the sea floor to 20,000 feet. The project office carried the designator PM-11.
entities.tierRationale: Cluster, tier and C/A/D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-area52-2.md section 4.

claims.text: The programme has a dated origin and a named parent. 'The Deep-Submergence Systems Review Group (DSSRG) was established in April 1963 to (1) review the Navy's plans for the development and procurement of components and systems related to location, identification, rescue from and recovery of deep-submerged large objects from the ocean floor.' Then: 'In February 1964 the Group reported its findings and recommendations. After review of the report, the Secretary of the Navy assigned the responsibility for implementation of the program, which was renamed the Deep-Submergence Systems Project (DSSP), to the Navy's Special Projects Office.'

Planned force in 1965 was six rescue vehicles and four search vehicles operational by 1970.
claims.source: David Taylor Model Basin Report 1985, March 1965, DTIC AD-614632, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0614632

claims.text: The 20,000 foot capability belongs to the search vehicle, not the rescue vehicle. The search vehicle's primary missions are 'to search the ocean bottom to depths of 20,000 ft for either large or small objects and to recover small objects either by actually lifting them or by making an attachment to the object so that a surface lift, or buoyancy lift, can be accomplished', while the study states of the rescue vehicle that 'Only operating depths of 6000 ft are considered in this study.'

claims.text: The Navy's own 1967 account gives the launch year and the organisational home: 'The Deep Submergence Systems Project (DSSP) was established as a separate Project within the Naval Material Command. The DSSP was launched in 1964 to develop and deliver to the fleet new underwater capabilities: a new rescue system, a large object salvage system, diver tools, the techniques of saturated diving for extended operations on the continental shelf, and new submersible vehicles capable of searching the ocean floors.' The same report describes a planned Deep Submergence Search Vehicle 'whose mission is ultimately to conduct sea floor search to a depth of 20,000 ft, providing coverage of 98 percent of the worlds oceans.'

claims.text: Two real recoveries frame the programme in the Navy's own telling: the loss of USS Thresher in 1963, whose hull was located in 8,500 ft of water after the casualty 'focused national attention on Navy capabilities underwater', and the 1966 loss of an unarmed nuclear weapon off the Mediterranean coast, located on the sea floor by ALVIN and recovered by the unmanned vehicle CURV.

entities.label: Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee (USIB)
entities.sub: Standing USIB committee, renamed from the Scientific Intelligence Committee in 1974; chartered to form a community position on unidentified foreign activities and anomalies
entities.desc: STIC was the United States Intelligence Board's standing committee on scientific and technical intelligence, renamed from the Scientific Intelligence Committee by a charter of 23 October 1974 to reflect a shift of emphasis toward technology. Its operating precept was early warning of foreign scientific or technical advances affecting national security, and it advised, and coordinated collection and production for, the USIB in those areas. Its charter lists among its Priority Group II objectives the assessment and establishment of an Intelligence Community position regarding certain unidentified foreign activities and anomalies in the science and technology area, which places a standing community mechanism for exactly that question inside the intelligence structure of the 1970s. A Letter of Instruction of 3 August 1975 shows the committee still operating under the Deputy to the DCI for the Intelligence Community and reorganising its subgroups.

entities.label: Belgian Air Force F-16 intercept and the 1989-90 Belgian wave
entities.sub: NATO air force scrambled, recorded and reported; the MoD was not told at the time
entities.desc: In March 1990 the Belgian Air Force scrambled F-16 fighters against objects reported by police officers and others during a wave of sightings running through 1989 and 1990. The Belgian Air Force sent the UK Ministry of Defence an official statement about it in November 1993, and a four-page account by General Wilfried de Brouwer, Chief of Operations of the Belgian Air Staff, sits in a released MoD file: it says the F-16 pilots obtained radar lock-ons and could not explain the phenomena, and that the events remain unexplained. The Secretary of State for Defence later told Lord Hill-Norton that the MoD had not been informed at the time and that there was no threat to the UK. This node rests on The National Archives' own guide to the August 2009 release and on Project Condign Volume 2; neither Belgian file nor either MoD file has been opened, and the node's date is the date the records give for the imagery and the scramble, not a date taken from a broadcast.

entities.label: Cosford incident, 30-31 March 1993
entities.sub: More than 30 sightings in six hours; ACAS briefed on an evasion, then attributed to a rocket re-entry
entities.desc: On the night of 30 to 31 March 1993 more than thirty reports of bright lights over central England reached the Ministry of Defence within about six hours, from police officers and military witnesses including a police patrol at RAF Cosford. The MoD's UFO desk had the RAF replay radar tapes and nothing unusual had been detected. The Assistant Chief of the Air Staff, Sir Anthony Bagnall, was nonetheless briefed that there was evidence a UFO had evaded UK defences, and The National Archives' own guide to the release then records that the majority of the sightings turned out to have been caused by the re-entry of the Russian rocket that launched the Cosmos 2238 satellite. The node carries both halves because the second is the finding: the internal alarm and the mundane resolution are in the same paragraph of the same official guide. The file is DEFE 24/2086; the paper piece is closed until 2078 and only a redacted digital copy is open.

entities.label: US Army Intelligence and Security Command (INSCOM)
entities.sub: Army intelligence major command; ran the psychoenergetics effort as a special access programme, 1977-1985
entities.desc: INSCOM is the United States Army's intelligence and security major command, headquartered in this period at Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia, with subordinate elements at Fort George G. Meade. Its own documents date its exploitation of psychoenergetics to Project GRILL FLAME in 1977, undertaken after the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence and the commanding general agreed that INSCOM would check out the phenomenon and that Army Intelligence would obligate seventy-five thousand dollars for an SRI International selection and training programme. The successor project, CENTER LANE, was run from the Security Support Detachment of the 902d Military Intelligence Group at Fort George G. Meade under a special access programme designated by the Secretary of the Army, with a category-three access caveat on every page. INSCOM's commanding general recommended ending the Army's involvement in July 1984 and, on 2 March 1985, notified the Department of the Army of the project's deactivation and of the attachment of its assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency under operational control. The command's 1977 establishment order has not been opened; the dateStart above is the year INSCOM's own memorandum gives for the start of the work, not for the command.

entities.label: DoD special access programme governance change, 5 January 1994
entities.sub: SAPOC, Senior Review Group and SAPCO stood up under the Deputy Secretary of Defense
entities.desc: On 5 January 1994 the Deputy Secretary of Defense changed the Department's special access programme management and control structures, standardising the approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring of SAPs through a Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, with a Senior Review Group established to support the SAPOC principals and a Special Access Program Coordinating Office staffing both. By November 1994 the committee was chaired by Deputy Secretary John Deutch with the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Technology, the Under Secretary for Policy, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Assistant Secretary for C3I as permanent, non-delegable members. The Joint Security Commission, reporting to the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence on 28 February 1994, described the committee as recently formed and supported it. This node exists because the board's sapoc node dates the committee to a 2010 directive, and the 2010 issuance re-established rather than created it.

The plan standardized and formalized the SAP approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring process through the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC). A Senior Review Group (SRG) was established to support the SAPOC principals.' Tier 2 because the text opened is a transcription published by the Federation of American Scientists and no scan of the original bulletin was found from this environment.

BGEN Mike Kostelnik, OUSD(A&T), serves as both member and executive secretary to the SAPOC in his capacity as director of the SAPCO (SAP Coordinating Office). SAPOC membership is not further delegable.'
claims.source: Deputy Secretary of Defense, SAPOC Information Bulletin, November 1994, https://sgp.fas.org/othergov/sapoc.html

entities.label: Armed Forces Special Weapons Project
entities.sub: Joint Army-Navy atomic energy organisation, 1946-1959; military successor to the Manhattan Engineer District
entities.desc: The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project was established by joint directive of the Secretaries of War and the Navy, effective midnight 31 December 1946, to carry on the military service functions of the Manhattan Project that were retained under armed forces control when the Atomic Energy Commission took the civil ones. It reported directly to the Army Chief of Staff and the Chief of Naval Operations, its Chief and Deputy Chief sat on the Military Liaison Committee to the AEC, and its funds came by working fund advances from the AEC out of money formerly available to the Manhattan Project. Major General Leslie R. Groves became its first Chief on 28 February 1947. It was redesignated the Defense Atomic Support Agency in 1959 and, through DNA and DSWA, is the ancestor of the Defense Threat Reduction Agency.

claims.text: The charter is reproduced in the Department of Defense's own agency history: 'The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project established by joint directive of the Secretaries of War and Navy, effective as of midnight 31 December 1946, will operate directly under the Chief of Staff and the Chief of Naval Operations.'

claims.text: AFSWP took the military half of the Manhattan Project. The charter makes it 'responsible for carrying on the military service functions of the Manhattan Project retained under control of the armed forces', including military participation in the development of atomic weapons of all types in coordination with the Atomic Energy Commission, and assigns to it as of 31 December 1946 the Army units that had been assigned to the Manhattan Engineer District.

entities.label: Defense Threat Reduction Agency
entities.sub: DoD combat support agency, 1998 to present; heir of AFSWP, DASA, DNA and DSWA
entities.desc: The Defense Threat Reduction Agency was established in the Department of Defense as a combat support agency effective 1 October 1998 by DoD Directive 5105.62 of 30 September 1998, consolidating the Defense Special Weapons Agency, the On-Site Inspection Agency, the Defense Technology Security Administration and elements of the Office of the Secretary of Defense concerned with arms control. Its own agency history traces an unbroken line from the Manhattan Engineer District through AFSWP, DASA, DNA and DSWA, and calls it the nation's oldest defense agency. Its published Privacy Act inventory records that it holds nuclear test participation and exposure records reaching back to 1945 and human radiation experimentation records reaching back to 1944. The National Archives holds the AFSWP, DASA and DNA era textual records as Record Group 374 and names the Atomic Energy Commission's own records, Record Group 326, as a separate related group.

entities.label: Office of Naval Research
entities.sub: Created 1 August 1946 in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy; the Navy's research contracting authority
entities.desc: The Office of Naval Research was created by Act of Congress on 1 August 1946, the same day as the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, inside the Office of the Secretary of the Navy. It is headed by a Chief of Naval Research appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, advised by a civilian Naval Research Advisory Committee of up to fifteen preeminent scientists, and it holds the Navy's authority over patents, inventions and royalties. The Act frees its research contracting from five named sections of the Revised Statutes and from performance bonds, lets appropriated research funds stay available for four further years, and authorises the transfer to it of the Naval Research Laboratory and the Special Devices Division.

claims.text: The Act creates the office inside the Secretary's own office: 'there is hereby created and established in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy an Office of Naval Research', charged with the encouragement, promotion, planning, initiation and coordination of naval research, and with the supervision, administration and control of Navy activities relating to patents, inventions, trade-marks, copyrights and royalty payments.
claims.source: An Act to establish an Office of Naval Research in the Department of the Navy, Public Law 79-588, ch. 727, H.R. 5911, 60 Stat. 779, sec. 1, approved 1 August 1946, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: Its head is a presidential appointee confirmed by the Senate. Section 2 provides for a Chief of Naval Research 'appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, for a term of not to exceed three years, from among officers not below the grade of commander on the active list of the Navy.'
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779, sec. 2, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: The Act exempts ONR research contracting from ordinary law. Section 6 permits contracts for research 'without performance or other bonds' and without regard to five named sections of the Revised Statutes, and advance and progress payments without regard to another, while expressly barring cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contracting. Section 5(b) keeps obligated research appropriations available for expenditure for four years after the fiscal year for which they were appropriated.
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779-780, secs. 5(b) and 6, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: Section 7 authorises the Secretary of the Navy to transfer research and development functions from the bureaus to ONR together with personnel, buildings, facilities and other property, 'including without limitation the Special Devices Division and the Naval Research Laboratory.'
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 780, sec. 7, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

entities.label: British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement (UKUSA), 5 March 1946
entities.sub: STANCIB and the London SIGINT Board; twelve paragraphs; the clause forbidding disclosure of its own existence
entities.desc: The agreement signed on 5 March 1946 between the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board and the London Signal Intelligence Board is the founding instrument of what became the Five Eyes arrangement. In twelve paragraphs it commits the two sides to unrestricted exchange of the products of collection, traffic analysis, cryptanalysis, decryption and translation of foreign communications, and of the methods and techniques behind them, with withholdings to be notified and kept to a minimum. It defines third parties as everyone outside the United States, the British Empire and the Dominions, forbids either party from acting toward a third party without the other's agreement, and makes it contrary to the agreement to reveal that the agreement exists at all. It supersedes all previous British and United States agreements in the field and is terminable by either party on notice. Nothing in it concerns anomalous objects or their recovery.

claims.text: The agreement is between the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board, representing the U.S. State, Navy and War Departments and all other U.S. Communication Intelligence authorities which may function, and the London Signal Intelligence Board, representing the Foreign Office, Admiralty, War Office, Air Ministry and all other British Empire Communication Intelligence authorities which may function.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 1, NSA UKUSA release copy, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The agreement forbids disclosure of itself: 'It will be contrary to this agreement to reveal its existence to any third party whatsoever.' Third parties are defined as all individuals or authorities other than those of the United States, the British Empire and the British Dominions.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 5(a) and its footnote, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The exchange is defined by operation, not by target. Paragraph 3(a) commits both parties to exchange the products of collection of traffic, acquisition of communication documents and equipment, traffic analysis, cryptanalysis, decryption and translation, and acquisition of information regarding communication organisations, practices, procedures and equipment. Paragraph 4 extends the exchange to the methods and techniques involved, in both cases unrestricted except on notified withholding.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, paras. 3 and 4, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The Dominions are held between the parties and the excluded world: 'While the Dominions are not parties to this agreement, they will not be regarded as third parties.' The London SIGINT Board is to keep the United States informed of arrangements with Dominion agencies, and STANCIB is to complete no arrangement with any Canadian agency without first obtaining the London Board's views.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 6, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The document is signed for the London Signal Intelligence Board by an officer described as Colonel, British Army General Staff, whose name the scan does not render legibly, and for the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board by Hoyt S. Vandenberg, Lieutenant General, GSC, as Senior Member. It is dated 5 March 1946 and its pages carry the NSA declassification exemption marking NSA25X6 with EO 1.4.(d).
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, signature page and page markings, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The agreement contains nothing about anomalous objects. A search of the extracted text of all six numbered pages for 'flying', 'saucer', 'unidentified', 'aerial phenomen' and 'anomalous' returns no occurrence of any of them. The instrument is a communications intelligence sharing agreement and its secrecy clause covers its own existence, not any subject matter beyond communications.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, full text, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

entities.label: Armed Forces Institute of Pathology
entities.sub: DoD pathology institute created by 10 U.S.C. 176 in 1976; disestablished in part by BRAC 2005, its Tissue Repository preserved by statute
entities.desc: A Department of Defense pathology institute created by statute in 1976 as a joint entity of the three military departments, with a lineage the 2005 BRAC Commission traces to the Army Medical Museum of 1862. The 2005 BRAC recommendation on Walter Reed disestablished all of its elements except the National Medical Museum and the Tissue Repository, and directed that its unspecified capabilities be absorbed into other DoD, Federal or civilian facilities; Congress then required a Joint Pathology Center in the FY2008 National Defense Authorization Act. Its authorising statute, 10 U.S.C. 176, was never repealed and remains in force. It is drafted here for that documented custody chain over a national tissue repository, not for the claim that put it into the corpus.

A 2 for a joint entity of the three military departments under the Secretary of Defense. D 1 because the only thing said about it here is Richard Doty's, and he corrects himself inside the same passage. Tier C: nothing opened connects the Institute to this board's subject.

timeline.label: Truman creates the Central Intelligence Group and the post of Director of Central Intelligence
timeline.text: A Presidential directive on the coordination of foreign intelligence activities provides that personnel assigned from State, War and the Navy 'shall collectively form a Central Intelligence Group and shall, under the direction of a Director of Central Intelligence, assist the National Intelligence Authority', the Director to be designated by the President and to sit as a non-voting member of the Authority. Rear Adm. Sidney W. Souers is the first holder and signs as Director of Central Intelligence within two weeks.
timeline.source: Presidential Directive on Coordination of Foreign Intelligence Activities, 22 January 1946, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 71, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d71

timeline.label: The British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement is signed
timeline.text: STANCIB and the London Signal Intelligence Board sign a twelve-paragraph agreement for unrestricted exchange of the products and methods of communications intelligence. It defines third parties as everyone outside the United States, the British Empire and the Dominions, and states that 'It will be contrary to this agreement to reveal its existence to any third party whatsoever.' A search of all six numbered pages returns no occurrence of flying, saucer, unidentified, aerial phenomen or anomalous.
timeline.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, NSA UKUSA release copy, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

timeline.label: The Office of Naval Research is created, the same day as the Atomic Energy Act
timeline.text: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779, establishes an Office of Naval Research in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy, headed by a Chief of Naval Research appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. Section 6 frees its research contracting from five named sections of the Revised Statutes and from performance bonds; section 5(b) keeps obligated research appropriations available four further years. It carries the same approval date as the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 at 60 Stat. 755, not a date two days later.
timeline.source: An Act to establish an Office of Naval Research in the Department of the Navy, Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779, approved 1 August 1946, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

timeline.label: The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project takes effect, holding the military half of the Manhattan Project
timeline.text: AFSWP is established by joint directive of the Secretaries of War and the Navy 'effective as of midnight 31 December 1946', operating directly under the Army Chief of Staff and the Chief of Naval Operations and responsible for carrying on the military service functions of the Manhattan Project retained under armed forces control. The founding memorandum is signed on 29 January 1947 by Robert P. Patterson and James V. Forrestal; Major General Leslie R. Groves becomes first Chief on 28 February 1947. Its funds come by working fund advances from the Atomic Energy Commission out of money formerly available to the Manhattan Project.
timeline.source: War Department Memorandum No. 850-25-8, 18 March 1947, reproduced in Appendix D of Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, DTIC ADA412977, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

timeline.label: Truman establishes the Psychological Strategy Board by secret directive
timeline.text: A directive to the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence, classified secret, establishes a Board reporting to the National Security Council for the formulation of over-all national psychological objectives, policies and programmes. Its editorial footnote names the first Director: 'Gordon Gray, President of the University of North Carolina and former Secretary of the Army, was appointed Director of the new board.' The same directive forbids the Board and the Director to perform any psychological operations themselves.
timeline.source: Directive by the President to the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defense (Marshall), and the Director of Central Intelligence (Smith), 4 April 1951, FRUS 1951 vol. I doc. 16, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1951v01/d16

timeline.label: The Institute of Field Physics is incorporated, with an anti-gravity disclaimer written into its publicity
timeline.text: The Institute receives its certificate of incorporation and is placed inside the physics department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill under Bryce and Cecile DeWitt, funded principally by Agnew Bahnson. George Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company buy a Founder's Membership for 5,000 dollars. On John Wheeler's insistence a Protection Clause is attached to every publicity statement declaring that the work 'has no connection with so-called "anti-gravity research" of whatever kind and for whatever purposes'.
timeline.source: History of the Institute of Field Physics (1955-1959), Dean Rickles, UNC Chapel Hill Department of Physics and Astronomy department history, Section II, https://physics.unc.edu/department-history/section-ii/

timeline.label: CIA resolves to route Keyhoe's UFO inquiries to the Air Force, and to make it a precedent
timeline.text: A CIA memorandum for record on 'Comments on Letters Dealing with Unidentified Flying Objects' notes that the Air Force was 'most insistent' on answering his letters itself, that 'the Air Force is endeavoring to impress upon Major Keyhoe and others in a similar position, that his office is the proper place to come for such information', and concludes: 'I think we can use this procedure as a precedent henceforth in all inquiries regarding UFO's.'
timeline.source: CIA memorandum for record, 'Comments on Letters Dealing with Unidentified Flying Objects', CIA reading room document 0005516043, reading-room date 4 April 1958, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0005516043

timeline.label: ATIC is discontinued and the Foreign Technology Division is constituted the same day
timeline.text: The Air Force organizational-history record gives a discontinuation and a new constitution rather than a renaming: 'Air Technical Intelligence Center established 21 May 1951; redesignated Aerospace Technical Intelligence Center, 21 September 1959; discontinued 1 July 1961. Foreign Technology Division constituted, activated, and organized 1 July 1961', with the mission and resources absorbed by FTD on that date. The board's prose in more than one node says ATIC 'became' FTD; the record calls it a discontinuation and an absorption. Carried at Tier 2 because the compilation is a private site citing the Air Force Historical Research Agency, whose own pages return 403 to this environment.
timeline.source: AEROSPACE TECHNICAL INTELLIGENCE CENTER, Department of the Air Force Organizational Histories compilation, sourced to the Air Force Historical Research Agency, https://www.usafunithistory.com/PDF/A-E/AEROSPACE%20TECHNICAL%20INTELLIGENCE%20CENTER.pdf

timeline.label: AFR 80-17 assigns the Blue Book effort to the Foreign Technology Division by name
timeline.text: Air Force Regulation 80-17 provides that 'The Air Force Systems Command will support the program with current resources within the Foreign Technology Division (FTD) at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, to continue Blue Book effort', requires FTD to 'Analyze and evaluate all information and evidence reported to bases on those UFOs which are not identified at the base level', and requires FTD to 'prepare a final case report on each sighting reported to it'. Six months earlier the USAF Scientific Advisory Board's ad hoc committee had recorded the resources behind the whole programme as 'only one officer, a sergeant, and secretary'.
timeline.source: Air Force Regulation 80-17, Research and Development - UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS (UFO), 19 September 1966, https://nicap.org/afr80-17.htm

timeline.label: The USIB charters a standing committee tasked with anomalies by name
timeline.text: The charter of the Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee records the renaming from the Scientific Intelligence Committee and lists among its Priority Group II objectives the 'Assessment and establishment of an Intelligence Community position regarding certain unidentified foreign activities and anomalies in the S&T area'. The committee advises the United States Intelligence Board and coordinates collection and production in those areas. Nothing in the charter mentions the Robertson Panel.
timeline.source: CHARTER, Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee, 23 October 1974, CIA-RDP79M00098A000500020010-4, https://archive.org/download/cia-readingroom-document-cia-rdp79m00098a000500020010-4/cia-rdp79m00098a000500020010-4_djvu.txt

timeline.label: INSCOM puts a written assessment of the Monroe Institute's Gateway Process on the record
timeline.text: A twenty-nine page memorandum from the US Army Operational Group, US Army Intelligence and Security Command, Fort George G. Meade, analyses the Gateway Experience on tasking from its own commander and states that it is meant as 'a useful guide for other USAINSCOM personnel who are required to take the Gateway training or work with Gateway materials'. It names remote viewing as a follow-on technique inside the method and concludes that there is 'a sound, rational basis in terms of physical science parameters for considering Gateway to be plausible in terms of its essential objectives'.
timeline.source: Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process, US Army Operational Group, INSCOM, 9 June 1983, CIA-RDP96-00788R001700210016-5, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-cia-rdp96-00788r001700210016-5

timeline.label: INSCOM deactivates CENTER LANE and attaches its assets to DIA
timeline.text: INSCOM notifies the Department of the Army of 'the deactivation of the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project, the attachment OPCON of CENTER LANE assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the retirement of CENTER LANE as an active project nickname', and asks HQDA to officially discontinue CENTER LANE 'as a Secretary of the Army designated Special Access Program'. The initiative was INSCOM's own: its commanding general had recommended discontinuing the work in July 1984.
timeline.source: Letter, Deactivation of INSCOM CENTER LANE Project (ICLP) as a Special Access Program (SAP) (U), 2 March 1985, CIA-RDP96-00789R002100120002-4, https://archive.org/download/cia-readingroom-document-cia-rdp96-00789r002100120002-4/cia-rdp96-00789r002100120002-4_djvu.txt

timeline.label: The Belgian Air Force scrambles F-16s during the Belgian wave
timeline.text: The National Archives' guide to the MoD UFO files opened in August 2009 states that the files 'reveal how in March 1990 the Belgian Air Force scrambled F-16 fighters to intercept UFOs reported by police officers and others', and places a four-page account by General Wilfried de Brouwer, Chief of Operations, Belgian Air Staff, in DEFE 24/1960, confirming that the F-16 pilots obtained radar lock-ons but could not explain the phenomena. Malcolm Rifkind later told Lord Hill-Norton that the MoD was not informed at the time.
timeline.source: The National Archives, Highlights Guide to the MoD UFO files opened 17 August 2009, https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/aug-2009-highlights-guide.pdf

timeline.label: More than thirty sightings over central England in six hours, then a rocket re-entry
timeline.text: The MoD's UFO desk had the RAF replay radar tapes and 'found nothing unusual had been detected'; the Assistant Chief of the Air Staff was nonetheless briefed 'that there was evidence a UFO had evaded UK defences'. The same official guide then records that 'It soon emerged that the majority of sightings were caused by the Russian rocket that launched the Cosmos 2238 satellite, re-entering the earths atmosphere.' Both halves are in one paragraph of one guide.
timeline.source: The National Archives, Highlights Guide to the MoD UFO files opened 17 August 2009, https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/aug-2009-highlights-guide.pdf

The plan standardized and formalized the SAP approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring process through the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC). A Senior Review Group (SRG) was established to support the SAPOC principals.' The Joint Security Commission called the committee a 'recent formation' on 28 February 1994.
